headerBody: France: Tourist Scams is part of the tabiji.ai Travel Safety Series. Every scam is documented against French police and consumer-protection sources — the Préfecture de Police de Paris and the DGCCRF anti-fraud directorate — plus r/ParisTravel reports and verified local news from Le Parisien, Nice-Matin and La Provence. Each one is drawn as a Hergé-style ligne-claire comic so you recognize the setup on sight.
quadHead: Four ways France catches tourists off guard.

quad.title: The Gold Ring Trick
quad.tl: A woman "finds" a gold ring at your feet on the Pont des Arts, presses it into your hand as a gift, then asks for €10–€20 — the ring is brass-plated junk worth pennies.

quad.title: The CDG Airport Taxi
quad.tl: A well-dressed man inside CDG arrivals offers a €70 ride, then demands €200 at your hotel citing "tolls and airport fees" — the official fixed fare from the rank outside is €56.

quad.title: The Promenade Water Bill
quad.tl: Tourist-strip restaurants on the Promenade des Anglais quietly swap the tap-water "carafe d'eau" you're entitled to for €6–€8 bottled water you never ordered, then stack hidden cover charges onto the bill.

quad.title: The Scooter Watch Snatch
quad.tl: Scooter crews on the Promenade des Anglais and at luxury-hotel entrances pull alongside, rip a watch off your wrist in a five-second snatch, and are gone before you react.

body: France: Tourist Scams is part of the tabiji.ai Travel Safety Series. Every scam is documented against French police and consumer-protection sources — the Préfecture de Police de Paris and the DGCCRF anti-fraud directorate — plus r/ParisTravel reports and verified local news. Not a recycled blog list.

191 specific scams across Paris, Nice, Marseille, Lyon and 12 more cities. The exact scripts, the red flags that give them away, and the French phrases that shut them down — with phonetics and français you can show on your phone.

Scams evolve, so the book is re-researched and updated every year — when a new edition ships, it appears in your Kindle library. Built for the traveler who wants to move through France relaxed, not braced.
